locator.work: Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (with The English Physician Enlarged), new edn. 1850 — Project Gutenberg eBook #49513, public domain
locator.heading: Herb

source_text:
THIS is so frequently known to be an inhabitant in almost every garden,
that I suppose it needless to write a description thereof.

_Time._] It flowers in June and July.

_Government and virtues._] It is under the dominion of Jupiter. The
ordinary Costmary, as well as Maudlin, provokes urine abundantly,
and moistens the hardness of the mother; it gently purges choler
and phlegm, extenuating that which is gross, and cutting that which
is tough and glutinous, cleanses that which is foul, and hinders
putrefaction and corruption; it dissolves without attraction, opens
obstructions, and helps their evil effects, and it is a wonderful
help to all sorts of dry agues. It is astringent to the stomach, and
strengthens the liver, and all the other inward parts; and taken in
whey works more effectually. Taken fasting in the morning, it is very
profitable for pains in the head that are continual, and to stay, dry
up, and consume all thin rheums or distillations from the head into
the stomach, and helps much to digest raw humours that are gathered
therein. It is very profitable for those that are fallen into a
continual evil disposition of the whole body, called Cachexia, but
especially in the beginning of the disease. It is an especial friend
and helps to evil, weak and cold livers. The seed is familiarly given
to children for the worms, and so is the infusion of the flowers
in white wine given them to the quantity of two ounces at a time;
it makes an excellent salve to cleanse and heal old ulcers, being
boiled with oil of olive, and Adder’s tongue with it, and after it is
strained, put a little wax, rosin, and turpentine, to bring it to a
convenient body.

pubmed.relevance_note: Compares chemical profiles and biological activity of C. segetum relative to related chrysanthemums, noting potential bioactive constituents relevant to traditional applications.

evidence.summary: Evidence for Chrysanthemum segetum is limited to a 2009 study comparing its chemical and biological properties with related species. The study highlights the presence of bioactive constituents like sesquiterpene lactones, which may underpin traditional uses regarding head pains or inflammatory conditions, though specific clinical data for this taxon remains sparse.

No specific PubMed documents were retrieved for Matricaria chamomilla in this search. While widely studied elsewhere for headache relief and digestive issues, the current evidence set contains no records to support or refute its traditional uses for rheums, head pains, or urine retention within the scope of these results.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence for Chrysanthemum segetum and Matricaria chamomilla is limited to chemical comparisons (PMID:19173127) or absent. No clinical data supports historical claims for urine retention, hardness of the mother, or specific humoral treatments.
concordance.uncertainty: High uncertainty due to lack of modern clinical trials and potential misidentification of 'Herb' as a generic term covering multiple taxa.
caveats: Historical terms like 'hardness of the mother' are obsolete medical concepts.
Taxonomic resolution confidence varies between 0.9 and 0.95.
